body:
I don't know whether keyboards or IMEs support, but adding `inputmode="numeric"` would be nicer for this case?

I've personally encountered such input requiring ASCII numeric characters while using my Japanese IME. so I understand your frustration. However, I'm afraid that silently changing the script type on input after typed without clear guidance might further confuse users.

I think at a minimum we should test that the `value` setter does not accept non-ASCII. That's weird.

I could see doing more. We currently have this note at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#number-state-(type=number):

> This specification does not define what user interface user agents are to use; user agent vendors are encouraged to consider what would best serve their users' needs. For example, a user agent in Persian or Arabic markets might support Persian and Arabic numeric input (converting it to the format required for submission as described above). Similarly, a user agent designed for Romans might display the value in Roman numerals rather than in decimal; or (more realistically) a user agent designed for the French market might display the value with apostrophes between thousands and commas before the decimals, and allow the user to enter a value in that manner, internally converting it to the submission format described above.

I think what @myakura might be hinting at is that it would be unexpected if you entered `１２３` in a numeric control to have it reflected back as `123`. However, preserving the input only works as long as you then not manipulate the value through stepping. So I'm not sure how much value there is in that. Perhaps if the Japanese locale always formatted numbers in full width that could be used for display, but either way you'll see some conversion happening.

cc @whatwg/forms @whatwg/i18n

> I don't know whether keyboards or IMEs support, but adding inputmode="numeric" would be nicer for this case?

Thank you. That's a good point.

Just to clarify: currently, `inputmode="numeric"` is defined in the HTML specification as a hint for virtual keyboards only. It does not affect IME behavior on desktop platforms.

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#input-modalities:-the-inputmode-attribute

For example, when I tested this in Chrome 137 on macOS and Windows, setting `inputmode="numeric"` did not change the input mode of the Japanese IME — it remained in its previous state (e.g., full-width input). So full-width digits like `２３４` could still be entered without any restriction. (though they won’t be reflected in the input's value).

Because of this, `inputmode` alone doesn't prevent the issues we're trying to address here — such as full-width input being silently rejected by `<input type="number">`.

@annevk Thank you again for your insights.

As the conversation has progressed, I realized that there are actually two distinct (but related) topics:

1. **Normalization during native input** (typing/pasting): Whether the HTML specification should explicitly allow (or recommend) user agents to normalize full-width characters like `２３４`, `－`, or `．` during user input into `<input type="number">`.   -- This is the main focus of this proposal.

2. **Programmatic `.value` assignment**: Whether assigning a full-width string to `.value` (e.g., `input.value = '２３４'`) should be accepted.  According to the current HTML specification, the value must be a valid number string, so full-width characters would not be considered conforming.  It seems that only Gecko currently accepts this input, which may be worth discussing separately to determine if this behavior aligns with the spec.

Out of respect for scope (and your help in shaping this proposal), I’d like to keep this issue focused on the native input case (1).  
The discussion about programmatic assignment — including related Web Platform Tests (WPT) — would be better handled in a separate issue.

If you're interested in exploring (2) further, I’d be happy to open that follow-up issue.

Very nicely written issue @kyouhei-horizumi .  Thanks for raising this.

I put together a very simple codepen at https://codepen.io/r12a/pen/PwqVJym.  

I noticed, while playing with it, that if you increment/decrement the number in Firefox the full-width characters are replaced by proportionally-spaced ones.  I therefore have a question for you: I wonder whether this conversion should occur _as the user types_, rather than after using controls to change the number. In other words, as the user types full-width digits, the form control automatically converts to and displays ASCII digits(same for dashes and dots), ie. the user would never see the fullwidth glyphs even though they are typing them.

The issue could be extended to cover many other scripts which have their own digits. For example, the behaviour noted for Japanese above appears to apply also to, say, the Arabic digits ١٢٣٤: (and other scripts, except for some recently encoded ones) Firefox displays and recognizes the native digits, but converts immediately to ASCII internally and replaces them with ASCII when incrementing using the control; Chrome 138 doesn't display or handle the native digits; and Safari displays the native digits in the form, but doesn't handle via JS and increments from 0.  It's not clear to me whether, for those scripts, changing the encoded code points for display is a good idea — there is, of course, a significant difference in shapes between native and ASCII digits that is not relevant to the case for Japanese fullwidth numbers. Did you consider other native digits while fixing Chrome? 

(There are other issues to be taken into account for native digit representations, related to types of numbering, base, etc, but they are probably not relevant for this particular discussion, especially for modern usage.)

> If you're interested in exploring (2) further, I’d be happy to open that follow-up issue.

I think we should treat it as non-conforming and test it as such, but feel free to track that as a new issue if you wish.

Thanks for the suggestion. I went ahead and opened a follow-up issue as you mentioned: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11405

It focuses on whether such input is conforming under the current spec, which seems to be relevant to Gecko's current behavior.  
Would appreciate any thoughts you have there!

@r12a Thank you for raising this important question.

When implementing the normalization in Chrome, we focused specifically on full-width characters commonly produced by Japanese IMEs — namely, full-width digits, minus signs, and the full-width period. We did not consider other native digit systems like Arabic-Indic numerals at that time.

That said, we’ve since looked into how Gecko handles this and found that Firefox does appear to support a broader range of native digit systems. Interestingly, Gecko also includes test coverage for these numeral systems in its internationalization tests — for example, [this file](https://github.com/mozilla/gecko-dev/blob/ac5daf3f3d5f63a5e2358da214a6793d84770dbd/js/src/tests/test262/intl402/shell.js#L2228) shows how Firefox tests a wide range of numberingSystem values (like arab, deva, mymr, fullwide, and many more) against native digit input.

However, I think full-width is actually a different concept from Locale—it’s more about encoding and visual representation rather than culturally defined number systems.

We agree that this is a broader topic worth discussing.
Any decision to normalize input across different numeral systems would require more careful consideration, and potentially coordination with spec discussions.
Since most developers — myself included — aren't familiar with the keyboard input patterns and user expectations across different locales — for instance, how users in neighboring countries typically input numbers — we'd need input from a much broader community to make informed decisions about these behaviors.

I was [actioned](https://github.com/w3c/i18n-actions/issues/176) by the I18N WG with responding to this issue in our [2025-06-26](https://www.w3.org/2025/06/26-i18n-minutes.html#7130) call, where we discussed the issue.


There are several possible areas of interaction here:

1. The user types a number using their native or OSK keyboard.
2. The value of the `input` field as a locale-neutral value interpreted from user input or assigned via scripting
3. The field value is displayed elsewhere in the page.

This issue is mostly about the first of these items. Users might type locally-shaped digits using direct input or via an IME. This might be because they do not wish to change input modes, particularly when traversing a form. A common case here is that CJK users are often not thinking about wide-vs-narrow input. In such a case, the control wants to accept "wide" characters as-if the user had switched to ASCII (narrow) input. This may also apply to other native inputs, such as Arabic-Indic digits and the like (see Richard's comments). We observe that, in fact, a number of browsers accept non-ASCII digit input and canonicalize it internally (they even allow mixed script input)

In addition, we observe that certain Japanese applications want to mostly use _zenkaku_ (wide) characters for Latin script to match input requirements, such as in postal address forms. 

Currently, there is no way to _fully_ control re-display of the internally recognized numeric value, such as by setting `lang`. The `lang` attribute does control aspects of input _parsing_ (such as which character is a decimal separator). It's possible to make weird-looking combinations of local and non-local digits that work (such as the ASCII `5` and `1` mixed with Devanagari here):

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d92c4de8-ef96-4274-9ac7-aac60d02b6d6)

Recognized numeric input is converted to ASCII digits in the `value` because that's the wire format in HTML. This is actually a Good Thing, since the wire format should be locale-neutral. Consumers of the `value` can (and should) create localized representation via mechanisms such as `Intl.NumberFormat`, rather than relying on the the field's locale-neutral representation.

Elsewhere in the thread, there is a discussion of assigning the value using a string, such as `input.value = '２３４'`. This seems complicated. While it seems attractive to allow "native-like" value scripting, the interpretation of digits depends on Unicode's numeric value property while the format is vaguely dependent on decimal separators set in the locale.

Finally, the I18N WG tends to feel that input should continue to be somewhat accepting of native digits, separators, and numeric symbols ("minus sign") and clearly communicate the resulting value to the user. It's super inconvenient for users to have to switch input mode/mechanism just to input a number or to have to switch back to a native input mode when they traverse away from the number control. It should just work.
Thanks everyone. As sufficient time has passed for further input, I’ve opened PR #11616 with concrete spec text.

Gecko (Firefox) seems to handle user input as the following:

1. If the user input can be parsed with [rules for parsing floating-point number values](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/common-microsyntaxes.html#rules-for-parsing-floating-point-number-values), use the parsed result.
2. Otherwise parse the user input with locale-aware way (using ICU).
   * Full-width digits and symbols are parsed in this step.

Thus, both user input `1.234` and `1,234` on `<input type="number" lang="de-DE">` are parsed as number `1.234`.

I think this way (locale-aware parsing as a fallback of locale-neutral parsing) is good in that when user input is the same as `value` attribute value, the input's `value` is ensured not to change. It is confusing if user input `1.234` on `<input type="number" value="1.234" lang="de-DE">` is parsed as number `1234`.

It is very helpful to normalize full-width digits and symbols but I'm not sure it should be defined in HTML spec.

Changing CLDR and ICU may give benefits to not only users of web browsers but also users of other applications. For example, changing [a loose matching step of UTS #35](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr35/47/tr35.html#Loose_Matching)

> * Map all characters in [:Dash:] to U+002D HYPHEN-MINUS

to

> * Map all characters in [:Dash:] and U+30FC KATAKANA-HIRAGANA PROLONGED SOUND MARK to U+002D HYPHEN-MINUS

@nanto 
(Sorry for the late reply — I was attending a local conference.)

Thanks to you for raising this issue, and also thanks to those who shared their thoughts in the PR discussion.

In the PR discussion, hsivonen suggested that an explicit mapping table for these few characters would be clearer than a partial NFKC explanation. aphillips noted that while such a table may be a short-term solution, the longer-term direction should be to get this handled in CLDR/ICU, so that the benefit extends beyond HTML.
(See PR #11616 for details.)

I’ll keep an eye on the PR discussion.

@xfq 
> What about the fullwidth plus sign?

Thanks for raising the U+FF0B (FULLWIDTH PLUS SIGN).
Our current patch intentionally focuses on characters that commonly appear unintentionally in CJK numeric entry and cause failed inputs today (full-width digits, full-width hyphen-minus, U+30FC as a minus look-alike, U+2212, full-width full stop).
In our JP field reports, a full-width plus hasn’t surfaced as a recurring pain point, mainly because **non-technical end users rarely need to type an explicit plus sign in `type="number"` fields.**

That said, since this discussion lives in the HTML Standard, I believe this is also the right place to **define where to draw the line between real-world behavior and the ideal model.**
Even if U+FF0B is not a common source of user errors today, we may still want to consider whether the spec should reflect **symmetry and conceptual completeness** rather than only current field evidence.

To make an informed decision, I’d love input from Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and Korean users/IME maintainers:

- In China, do common IMEs accidentally produce U+FF0B in numeric inputs?

In addition, I’d be very interested to hear whether the existing browser behavior—for example, in Chrome 141+ and other engines now accepting full-width digits and related characters in `type="number"` fields—has been working well for Chinese (and other CJK) users as well.
Were there similar input issues in Chinese environments that this change has already helped address, or was this mainly a Japan-specific problem that hasn’t been observed elsewhere?

Different input methods have different situations. As far as I know, the plus and minus signs in most Pinyin input method are ASCII characters. Japanese input methods are more likely to input full-width characters, including for the percent sign. Furthermore, in macOS, the Cangjie input method uses full-width characters for characters like plus and minus signs by default.

A typical scenario for using the plus sign is the telephone country code at the beginning of a phone number.
For a phone number you'd use `<input type=tel>`, maybe with `inputmode=numeric` (forgot if that combination is okay or redundant), not `<input type=number>`.

> For a phone number you'd use `<input type=tel>`, maybe with `inputmode=numeric` (forgot if that combination is okay or redundant), not `<input type=number>`.

Yes, I agree. What's the use case for hyphen? Is it usually used for negative numbers? Is it not necessary for positive numbers, as the plus sign is usually omitted?

The value space is defined at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#valid-floating-point-number which I suppose does argue for allowing + for (scientific) inputs such as 11.39e+5 although even there you could omit the + and get the same result. And yes, - is used for negative numbers.
If this is the case, the letter e may also appear in full-width.

Thanks for the discussion.
To summarize, the potentially relevant symbols from a symmetry standpoint are:

- `U+FF45` (`ｅ`)
- `U+FF25` (`Ｅ`)
- `U+FF0B` (`＋`).

I agree with this point.  
As there have been no objections so far, I’ve updated the PR description (as of 2025-10-28) to include a brief note summarizing the symmetry discussion.  
See: https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11616
